content: Non-sugar sweeteners (NSS) are substances used to impart sweetness to foods and beverages in very small quantities. Common examples of NSS include acesulfame K, aspartame, advantame, cyclamates, neotame, saccharin, sucralose, stevia, and stevia derivatives. Additionally, certain D-amino acids, plant proteins, and other extracts can also provide a sweet taste. NSS are defined as synthetic, naturally occurring, or modified non-nutritive sweeteners that are not classified as sugars. However, sugar alcohols and low-calorie sugars are not considered NSS. The acceptable daily intake (ADI) is a measure used to determine safe levels of NSS consumption. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have generally shown that NSS may have limited effects on glucose metabolism and can contribute to lower body weight when combined with energy restriction in the short term. However, there is no clear consensus on their long-term effects on weight loss, weight maintenance, or other health outcomes when consumed within the ADI. NSS interact with sweet-taste receptors to elicit a sweet taste, and they may produce similar physiological effects to some extent. However, NSS are not a homogeneous group of compounds. Each NSS has a unique chemical structure, which results in differences in sweetness intensity, sensory properties, and how they are processed by the body. These differences may lead to varying physiological effects in humans. Global trends in NSS use are not well-documented, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where robust longitudinal intake data are lacking. Nevertheless, available data suggest that the use of NSS in foods and beverages is significant and increasing in many regions, such as New Zealand, Norway, Slovenia, and the United States. This increase in NSS consumption corresponds with a decline in the consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages in some countries, such as the United States and Norway. The shift from free sugars to NSS is likely influenced by global efforts to reduce free sugar intake, particularly in settings implementing multiple policy actions to achieve this goal. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been actively involved in providing guidance on dietary goals to prevent obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Following the work of the 1989 WHO Study Group on Diet, Nutrition, and the Prevention of Chronic Diseases and the 2002 Joint WHO/FAO Expert Consultation, WHO updated its guidance on free sugar intake in 2015. Since then, there has been growing interest in whether incorporating NSS into policies and interventions aimed at reducing free sugar intake is effective and appropriate. Concurrently, the availability and use of NSS by consumers have increased. To address these developments, WHO conducted a systematic review of the evidence and issued guidance on NSS use through its guideline development process. This guideline complements other WHO recommendations on healthy diets, particularly the 2015 guideline on sugar intake. It is intended for the general population, including children, adults, and pregnant women, and is based on evidence of health effects of NSS use at levels considered safe by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA). The guideline does not aim to update or replace existing guidance on safe or maximal levels of NSS intake, which are based on toxicological assessments conducted by authoritative bodies. The guideline development process involved multiple contributors, including the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, the Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health, and external peer reviewers. The NUGAG Subgroup included experts from various disciplines and regions, ensuring a balanced gender mix and representation. Public consultations were held during the guideline's development to gather feedback from stakeholders and improve the clarity and usability of the document. Systematic review teams with expertise in review methodologies and subject matter were engaged to assess the health effects of NSS use. These teams worked closely with the WHO Secretariat to ensure the reviews met the needs of the guideline development process. Two public consultations were conducted, one during the scoping phase in 2016 and another on the draft guideline in 2022, to gather input on clarity, contextual issues, and implementation considerations. The WHO followed strict procedures for managing conflicts of interest among contributors, including members of the NUGAG Subgroup, external reviewers, and systematic review teams. Declared interests were reviewed before engagement and at each meeting, and internet searches were conducted to independently assess financial and intellectual interests. The overall procedures for managing conflicts of interest were in line with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The objective of this guideline is to provide evidence-informed recommendations on the use of NSS. It is intended for policymakers, program managers, health professionals, researchers, educators, and representatives of the food industry. The guideline supports the implementation of global health initiatives, including the prevention and control of NCDs, the UN Decade of Action on Nutrition, and the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to zero hunger and good health and well-being.
